concept: Each die is fair, but their total isn't: a sum that can be made in more ways comes up more often. Count ordered outcomes, not combinations: 7 has 6 of the 36, 12 has just 1.

misconceptions.label: Random means every outcome is equally likely
misconceptions.why_tempting: Fair dice feel like they should make every total equally fair too.
misconceptions.refutation: Two fair dice give 36 equally likely pairs, but totals collect different numbers of them: 7 gets 6 pairs, 2 and 12 get one each.
misconceptions.source_note: Gauvrit & Morsanyi 2014, 'The equiprobability bias...': people tend to judge 11 and 12 with two dice as equally likely

misconceptions.label: Count combinations, not orders
misconceptions.why_tempting: 5+6 and 6+5 look like the same roll, so 11 seems to have one way, like 12.
misconceptions.refutation: Paint one die red: red 5 + blue 6 and red 6 + blue 5 are different outcomes. 11 has 2 ways, 12 has 1, so 11 is twice as likely.
misconceptions.source_note: Leibniz wrote that 11 and 12 are equally probable since each 'can be made only one way'

items.prompt: Roll two fair dice and add them. Which total comes up most often?

options.text: Every total from 2 to 12 is equally likely
No total is favored; it's all luck

items.prompt: Roll two fair dice and add them. Which is more likely: a total of 11 or a total of 12?

options.text: Equally likely: 11 is 5+6 and 12 is 6+6, one pair each

items.prompt: Three fair dice. Ignoring order, a total of 9 can be made from six different sets of numbers (like 3+3+3 or 1+2+6), and so can 10 (like 3+3+4 or 1+3+6). Which total comes up more often?

options.text: Same: six sets of numbers each
